title: Forest Elephants and Football Games in Dzanga-Sangha

sections.heading: Body
sections.text:
Posted on January, 23 2026
Forest elephants at Dzanga Bai, Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas, Central African Republic. Photo Credit: ©Andy Issacson / WWF-US
“It is an exceptional place...the one and only place in the world where more than 100 forest elephants can be observed and counted at any given time,” says Felix Safouet.
Originally from Cameroon, Safouet lives in Bayanga village in the Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas, home to some of the Congo Basin’s most iconic species. Community members and tourists alike can see lowland gorillas, bongos and other rare wildlife in their natural habitat. The daily presence of African forest elephants, an emblematic species that's increasingly rare in the region, is part of what makes Dzanga-Sangha unforgettable.
Every day, elephants gather in a natural forest clearing called Dzanga Bai, searching the salt marsh for minerals they need to survive. On a platform overlooking the marsh, scientists study the behaviour of these gentle giants and identify individual visitors. Their findings inform conservation strategies to protect the species, which was defined as critically endangered in 2021.
Energy access supports conservation
But Safouet is a solar engineer, not a conservation scientist. His team helps power the study of elephants while making Dzanga-Sangha a more sustainable, healthy place for people and wildlife. The tool at their disposal: solar plants that harvest energy from the sun.
The elephant observation platform is one of 14 solar sites across the area today – together, they power nearly all electricity consumption within and surrounding the park. This includes the main office, an ecolodge for visitors, ten staff houses, a One Health medical laboratory, a nearby hospital and even a football field.
“Before the solar systems were installed, the park faced major operational challenges from its exclusive reliance on generators,” he said. The need for excessive fuel brought high costs and logistical headaches, including transporting fuel supplies on poor roads. Staff were also less productive with the limited electricity that these generators provided.
Solar power provides electricity at regular hours, ensuring seamless operations and eliminating reliance on fossil fuels. Solar also allows electrification of remote forest locations, where park staff used to have no power. “At the elephant observation platform, there was no way to recharge camera or laptop batteries, significantly limiting the effectiveness of monitoring and scientific data collection activities,” Safouet said. Now, scientists can continue their work without interruption. Eco-guard bases also have new charging for communications equipment maintaining 24/7 contact across the park.
Solar panels, on a garage roof, power the headquarters of the Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas in the Central African Republic. Photo credit: ©Stef de Béthune / APDS / WWF-CAR
But the road to solar wasn’t always smooth. The park first began experimenting with solar technology in 2010, and systems fell into disrepair from dead batteries and installation issues. One system had so many poor components and installation issues that it stopped working after just a few days – and the blue panels turned green from corrosion in the rainy climate. Without local capacity in solar engineering, some broken plants remained unfunctional for years.
It’s no wonder that local communities were skeptical of solar technology at first. “Perceptions of solar energy were still marked by a certain mistrust and a lack of information,” he said. “But with visible, concrete results ... attitudes have changed.”
How solar power is transforming daily life
Through WWF’s Energizing Communities and Conservation programme, WWF solar energy expert Jean-Philippe Denruyter began collaborating with local solar companies – including Safouet's organization – to refurbish abandoned solar systems. After several years of working closely together, Safounet became a permanent technician supporting Dzanga-Sangha's solar installations.
“Summing up such a fruitful and enriching partnership, spanning five years, is no easy task. Denruyter is a technical authority whose expertise and professional commitment I deeply respect,” said Safounet.
Together, Denruyter and Safouet maintain existing solar systems, and are drawing up plans for new ones, including an 81-kW solar power plant and mini-grid for the Bayanga village, where Safouet lives. This plant will bring renewable power to approximately 2000 households in the community. In recognition of the project, the President of the Central African Republic placed the plant’s first solar panel during his visit in November 2025.
Safouet finds no shortage of inspiration in his work electrifying remote communities and protecting nature. “Installing solar systems in places where no one would have imagined access to electricity is a huge source of motivation,” he said. “Knowing that I bring a smile to their faces and a different perspective on their way of life.”
Daily life for locals of Dzanga-Sangha looks different today. Community members play football at dusk, taking advantage of the field’s solar-powered lights. Most businesses have a small solar system installed, opting for cheap energy and clean air over expensive, polluting generators. Suspicion has transformed into confidence.
“This type of success has convinced me that solar energy represents much more than an alternative: it is a viable, sustainable and essential solution for countries where access to electricity remains very limited.”
But, once in a while, Safouet comes across a forest elephant during his maintenance work at the main office – a reminder of the many living beings that his work benefits. Here in Dzanga-Sangha, human and elephants alike can have a brighter future under the sun’s warm rays.
Felix Safouet conducts routine inspections and does maintenence of solar installations in the Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas. Photo Caption: ©APDS / WWF-CAR
WWF's Energizing Communities and Conservation (ECCo) programme has enabled 24+ solar projects to be set up in the Congo Basin, with Dzanga-Sangha at the heart of these installations. More solar upgrades and installations are in the works, including for field camps in the Republic of Congo, Salonga Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Campo Ma’an Park in Cameroon, and new batteries for WWF’s Libreville office in Gabon. This solar energy work is implemented under the supervision of the Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas, co-managed between WWF-Central African Republic office and the Central African Republic Ministry of Forest, Water, Hunting and Fishing.
For more information, contact Jean Philippe Denruyter at jdenruyter@wwf.eu
